title: When two words sound the same
goal: How one global solve decides who keeps a stroke: spelling, the star ladder, the marker stroke, names.

blocks.x: One primary stroke per word

A word gets exactly one primary single-stroke outline, never several to choose between. This page covers *which* word keeps a stroke when two or more want it. A word's extra one-stroke forms only take strokes left free by this settling. Multi-stroke backups are separate and unlimited: see [syllables and folding](#/ref/syllables).
Everything is settled together

Briefs, spelling and the star ladder are one pass. Every word's legal candidates go into one shared pool, and a single solve picks the assignment minimizing the whole dictionary's total cost, weighted by word frequency. A word's candidates:

items: a gold brief of its own (see [briefs](#/ref/briefs)), if it keys the first onset or pays for itself (see [faithful outlines](#/ref/collisions));
lyk's plain rules reading;
the spelling-told-apart variant for its sound-alike group (see [spelling](#/ref/spelling));
every brevity-shortened form (see [how short](#/ref/brevity));
the full star ladder, below;
for a word spelled with a literal trailing `s`, the same candidate again with a voiced `-Z` coda respelled `-S`.

blocks.x: The letter is decided by cost per word, not a blanket rule: *girls* is [[girls|TKPWEURLS]] with its [[-Z]] reading [[girls|TKPWEURLZ]] kept as an extra; *abhors* is [[abhors|PWHORS]].
A common word can lose an outline to another word if that makes the whole dictionary cheaper; a rare word's situation can move a common word to its next-cheapest candidate.
Words with no prose use stay behind the star

A word with **no prose use** is one nothing shows to be read in running text: a vocal noise or sound effect (*ugh*, *hmm*, *shh*, *brr*, *ooh*) or a stray string a pronunciation list carries (*ees*). Such a word competes only with its star ladder outlines, takes no family shape, no extra and no other-pronunciation entry, so it never holds a plain stroke a word that is used might want, and it still has an outline: *ees* is [[ees|AO*EZ]].

items: **Stays plain, always:** *oh*, *ah*, *eh*, *uh*, *um*, *yea*, *yeah*, *yeh*, *ok*, *okay*, *hey*, *wow*; and any word that occurs **3 or more times** in the prose of the five bundled books (*mr*, *mrs*, *dr*).

**Noise letters:** a run of three of one letter (*zzz*, *mmm*), or an exclamation's shape once repeated letters are cut to one (*ahh*, *ooh*, *ohh*, *uhh*, *ugh*, *hmm*, *shh*, *brr*, *grr*, *psst*, *tsk*, *pfft*, *argh*, *eww*).

**Stray string:** four letters or fewer, said fewer than 1,000 times in the frequency list, written by no steno dictionary (Plover, Lapwing or any other theory), and pronounced only by the fallback sources, not CMUdict.
A word with no star outline keeps whatever candidates it has. The current build flags about 560 words.

blocks.x: A rare word does not hold a common word's extra stroke

A common word keeps its plain rules reading and its gold briefs as [extras](#/ref/briefs) even when a cheaper outline is its primary: *ease* is [[ease|AEZ]], and [[ease|AOEZ]] (the reading by the sounds, Lapwing's too) is an extra. A rare word may not hold such a stroke as its primary. After settling, a word said at most **200** times in the frequency list that holds the stroke of one of another word's four cheapest extra options, where that word is said at least **30 times** as often, gives it up. The stroke goes to the common word as an extra, before short forms, other pronunciations and phrases take free strokes. The rare word takes its cheapest other candidate that is free (the star ladder: *ees* is [[ees|AO*EZ]]); with none left it has no primary and is written by its joined backups. A word said more than 200 times is never asked.
Faithful outlines: a dropped sound must pay

Plover's and Lapwing's briefs often leave out a sound at the start of the word: *grab* as `RAB`, *graph* as `TPWRAF` (a `G` with no `K`), *got* as `TKPOT` (a `G` as `TKP`). An outline is **faithful** when it writes every sound of the word's first onset with that sound's own keys, as the tables write them: `G` is all of `TKPW`, `J` is all of `SKWR`, `gr` is `TKPWR`, `bl` is `PWHR`. Vowels, the star, extra keys and the whole right hand are not checked. A sound at the end of the word may be dropped: [[find|TPAOEUD]] keys the F, the vowel and the D, not the N.
A gold outline that is unfaithful (as listed, or with its fragments dropped) is a candidate only if it **pays for itself**, in one of three ways:

items: **It saves a whole stroke.** It takes fewer strokes than every other candidate the word has. Cost ranks strokes first, then keys, so a drop that saves only keys within one stroke never pays: `TPWRAF` and the faithful `TKPWRAF` are both one stroke, so the faithful one wins. A long word whose faithful reading takes two or more strokes may drop a sound for one: [[request|KW]], [[describe|SKREU]].

**The word is among the commonest.** Its rank is below `faithful_exempt_rank` in `rules/plover.toml` (550). The commonest words keep their short briefs (*the*, *of*, *you*, also *make* `AEUBG`, *day* `AEU`, *give* `EUF`). A family member past that rank follows its root only if the root's shape keys the onset too. Several common words that drop a whole onset therefore stay: *great* `RAET`, *guy* `TKPAOEU`, *gone* `OPB`, *give* `EUF`, *gave* `AEUF`. Pinning *great* to `TKPWRAET` was measured and fails the Gutenberg guard (7.3% of words cost more than Plover) at ranks 550 and 650.
**A human pinned it.** A literal `[word]` outline in `rules/briefs.toml` (see [briefs](#/ref/briefs)), or a source named there, is always allowed. [[got|TKPWOT]] and [[find|TPAOEUD]] are pinned.

blocks.x: The rules' own reading is faithful by definition. The brevity ladder's one-stroke short forms (`shell`, `ends`, vowel-less skeleton, see [how short](#/ref/brevity)) are exempt: they save a stroke. A faithful outline can lose its stroke to a sound-alike, as any outline can: *graph* is [[graph|TKPWRAFR]] because the name *graff* holds `TKPWRAF`.
The exemption rank, measured

Measured with Plover and Lapwing as the only sources, before [other theories' briefs](#/ref/collisions) joined the pool. The ordering and the guard's cut-off at 550 are the same with them; the absolute numbers are those of the earlier pool.

Stroke count never moves; the taught set stays at 98.5%. Keys per word are what faithful onsets cost: 550 adds 0.02 keys a word (0.6%) and 1.2% comfort. The limit on lowering the exemption is the Gutenberg-prose guard in the test suite (at most 7.2% of words may cost more keys than Plover): rank 500 reads 7.2% rounded, just over; 550 passes. The keys-per-word guard (3.272 with 2% slack) holds at every rank in the table.
Other theories' briefs

Besides Plover and Lapwing, the generator reads fifteen more dictionaries as a pool of briefs: Stan's (a derivative of Magnum, Mark Kislingbury's theory), Josiah theory (a write-short theory with a dictionary of about 30,000 plain words; outlines on its extra `^` key do not exist on this layout and are skipped) and thirteen court-reporting theories published by Stenovations: Bryan, StarTran, Steno Foundation, The Steno Way, Tri-C, Pennsylvania Clinic, RealWrite, Robert Walsh Gonzales, San Antonio, South Coast College, StenEd, Stenograph and Thyra Ellis. Each is `data/dictionaries/theory-NAME.json`, downloaded by `fetch`; every `theory-*.json` found is merged into one list of outlines per word (`Gold::extra`). Not in the pool: Magnum's dictionary (sold with its book), Platinum's (members' download), Palantype (another layout).

**Their outlines must save a stroke.** An outline from these theories is a candidate only if it takes fewer strokes than every other candidate the word has (under any pronunciation), the rules' own reading included. They never replace a one-stroke outline the word already has. Neither the commonest-words exemption nor a faithful onset gets one in: a word that already fits one stroke keeps what Plover, Lapwing or the rules gave it. Without the rule a dozen theories handed *job* `KWROB`, *liquid* `KHREUD` and *dock* `TKAUBG`, each a key shorter and none predictable. Result: one-stroke words: *accuracy* (`ABG/+SEU` before) is [[accuracy|KRAES]], *added* (`AD/+-D`) is [[added|ATD]].

Cost is on the reading side. More words sit on irregular one-stroke briefs (*penguin* `PEPBG`, *incomplete* `*EUBG`), so the solver's weighted top-1 on backups falls a point (92.7% to 91.7%), each stroke carries more keys, and comfort per word is 0.4 worse. Taught outlines do not move. Plover's `PWHR-G` and similar family shapes can change hands: [[assembling|PWHR-G]] is one stroke now, so *building* is [[building|PW-LG]]. The Gutenberg-prose and keys-per-word guards hold unchanged.

**What does not save a stroke is used as an alternate.** The extras pass (the last, which only fills strokes nobody holds) also reads the other theories' one-stroke outlines for a word: the first onset must be keyed, no half of a multi-key sound may be in it, and it must be typable on lyk's layout (some theories use chords this layout cannot press). It adds them within three keys of the word's own outline, at most three extras per word with the word's own. They never become a primary, never take a stroke, never change a word's cheapest outline. About 1,000 alternates were added (24,652 to 25,672 extras); the other theories hold about 22,000 more unused one-stroke outlines, almost all for words that already have a one-stroke lyk outline; the filters, the three-extras cap and the key margin leave them out. Their multi-stroke outlines (about 219,000 unused) are not read; they were not sampled for quality.
What spelling decides

Spelling answers "who may propose this word's plain, unstressed-vowel reading", not "who wins it". *sail* (`!ai`) and *sale* (silent e) sound identical but spell the stressed vowel differently, so the rules write two outlines: [[sail|SAEUL]] for the `!ai` spelling and the shorter [[sale|SAEL]] for the silent e. Both are candidates. Which gets the longer or shorter form is decided by the same cost-and-frequency solve, usually giving the commoner member the cheaper one. See [spelling](#/ref/spelling) for how a sound becomes a spelling-told-apart variant.
The star ladder

When two words with the same spelling pattern want one stroke, the commoner keeps the plain stroke and the other falls down a ladder. Every word carries these four steps in its candidate pool, so a word that loses an outline falls to its next-cheapest option inside the same solve:

items: a star on the first stroke;
a star on the last stroke;
one extra star-marker stroke, [[+*]] after the outline;
two extra star-marker strokes.

blocks.x: Examples: [[night|TPHAOEUT]] and [[knight|TPHAO*EUT]]; [[flower|TPHROUR]] and [[flour|TPHRO*UR]]; [[pearl|PERL]] and [[peril|P*ERL]]; [[sweet|SWAOET]] and [[sweetie|SWAO*ET]].
A short form never takes an outline that any word's own rules produce; the forms a learner can work out stay theirs.
A star on a one-syllable stroke means the sound-alike

*doc* is [[doc|TKOBG]], so *dock* is [[dock|TKO*BG]]. *sock* is [[sock|SO*BG]] (and [[sobbing|SOBG]] is *sob* plus `-G`). A longer word's short form pays half a stroke on top of its cost to take a one-syllable stroke's star. A short form with another one-stroke form a key or two dearer leaves the star to the sound-alike. One that would otherwise be two strokes and is said far more often keeps it: *attack* is [[attack|TA*BG]], so *tack* is [[tack|TABG/+*]].
What a word falls to, in order
Cost decides: strokes first, then keys:

items: its own one-stroke reading;
a star on it;
a gold brief of its own that is still one stroke;

among two-stroke forms, the cheapest of: its stem-plus-suffix reading (*pearly* [[pearly|PERL/+EU]], once [[PERL]] is *pearl* and [[P*ERL]] is *peril*), a two-stroke gold brief, and its reading with one bare [[+*]] marker stroke.

blocks.x: The marker stroke is the last resort of a one-syllable word, and a rule, not a memorised fact: a stroke that is taken, starred and still taken is written again with [[+*]] after it. *suite* is [[suite|SWAOET/+*]] because [[SWAOET]] is *sweet* and [[SWAO*ET]] is *sweetie*. About 1,200 words end that way, almost all names and interjections (*uhh* [[uhh|U/+*]], *hah* [[hah|HA/+*]]).
Names

A name never outranks the word it sounds like. lyk writes a name as the ordinary outline of how it sounds, after the capitalize stroke [[KPA]]: *Matt* is [[KPA]] then *mat*'s stroke. A name and its sound-alike word compete for one stroke; the word gets it, since the name gets its capital from [[KPA]] either way.

items: Each name's count is cut to a tenth before ranking. A common name still outranks a rare word.
A name here is a word Plover and Lapwing only write capitalized (*Matt*, *Mike*, *Mary*, *America*, *Sunday*), never lowercase.
*mat* is [[mat|PHAT]] and *matt* is [[matt|PHAT/+*]].

Some names lose their one-stroke outline this way and are typed by syllables like any two-syllable word: *mary* is [[mary|PHAER/+EU]], since *marry* has [[marry|PHAER]] and *merry* has [[merry|PH*ER]].
